findings.title: Stack overflow from unbounded recursive deserialization of nested tables and arrays
findings.impact: A malicious AMQP server or a man-in-the-middle attacker can crash any client using this library by sending a crafted protocol message with deeply nested nested tables/arrays, causing denial of service.
findings.evidence: The readFieldValue() method at line 158 recursively deserializes untrusted AMQP protocol data. Case 'F' at line 181 calls readTable(), which at line 150 calls readFieldValue() again. Case 'A' at line 184 calls readArray(), which at line 245 calls readFieldValue() again. An attacker can craft a protocol message with deeply nested tables and arrays (e.g., table containing array containing table containing array...) to trigger unbounded recursion and exhaust stack memory, causing StackOverflowError.

findings.title: Integer overflow in timestamp multiplication without bounds checking
findings.impact: An attacker sending a malicious AMQP protocol message with a specially crafted timestamp value could cause integer overflow, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect time value. This could potentially be exploited in business logic that relies on timestamp ordering or validity, or could cause unexpected behavior in code that assumes timestamp validity.
findings.evidence: At line 269, the code reads an 8-byte long from the network and multiplies it by 1000 without overflow checking: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. If the long value read from the network is greater than Long.MAX_VALUE / 1000 (approximately 9223372036854775), the multiplication will silently overflow, wrapping to a negative value or causing unexpected behavior in Date constructor.

defects_to_look_for.mechanism: A length field read from untrusted input decides the size of a buffer, and that buffer is created before the corresponding payload has been shown to exist.
Decoding routines call one another in a cycle with nothing counting how deep the cycle has gone, so nesting in the input controls the depth.
